Blepharitis can lead to other eye problems, including:
- Stye. A stye is a red, painful bump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland.
- Chalazion. A chalazion is a hard, painless lump on the eyelid caused by a blocked oil gland. Often, this happens when you have a stye that doesn’t go away. It can make your eyelid swell and turn red. A chalazion will often go away on its own.
- Dry eye. Oil and flakes can build up in your tear film (a thin layer of tears across the surface of your eye). This can make your eyes feel dry. Or your eyes may feel watery or teary because your tears aren’t working correctly.
- Damage to the cornea. In severe cases, blepharitis can hurt your cornea (the clear outer layer at the front of your eye). This can happen because of swelling or irritation in your eyelids or eye lashes that grow in the wrong direction.
- Chronic (long-term) red eye. Blepharitis can make the white part of your eye look red all the time [nei_007_chunk_04].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

To prevent spreading if your pink eye is caused by an infection:
- Don’t share towels, bed sheets, or makeup [nei_046_chunk_01].
- Throw out tissues after wiping your eyes [nei_046_chunk_01].
- Wash your hands frequently [nei_046_chunk_01].

If your pink eye is caused by an allergen or irritant, try to avoid the allergen or irritant [nei_046_chunk_02].

If your pink eye is bacterial, antibiotics can speed up healing, but aren’t always needed [nei_046_chunk_02].

Go to the doctor if:
- You have a lot of pain in your eye [nei_046_chunk_02].
- Your eye is very red [nei_046_chunk_02].
- You notice a lot of mucus coming from your eyes [nei_046_chunk_02].
- Your vision is blurry or you’re sensitive to light — and it doesn’t get better when you wipe away discharge from your eye [nei_046_chunk_02].
- Your symptoms don’t get better after a few days — or they get worse [nei_046_chunk_02].
- You have a health condition that weakens your immune system [nei_046_chunk_02].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is a refractive error that makes nearby objects look blurry [nei_011_chunk_01]. It happens when the shape of the eye makes light focus behind the retina instead of on it [nei_011_chunk_01]. This can be caused by an eyeball that grows too short from front to back, or by problems with the shape of the cornea or lens [nei_048_chunk_02]. People with farsightedness can use eyeglasses, contact lenses, or surgery to see clearly [nei_011_chunk_01]. Symptoms may include trouble seeing things up close, eye strain, and headaches [nei_011_chunk_01]. Mild farsightedness may not cause any symptoms, so regular eye exams are recommended [nei_011_chunk_01].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

answer:
Eye doctors can check for Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) as part of a comprehensive dilated eye exam [nei_020_chunk_03]. This exam involves eye drops to widen the pupil, followed by checking the eyes for RP and other eye problems [nei_020_chunk_03]. The exam includes a visual field test to assess peripheral vision [nei_020_chunk_03].

Other tests used to diagnose RP are Electroretinography (ERG), which measures how well the retina responds to light [nei_020_chunk_03]. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is another test that uses light waves to take a detailed picture of the retina [nei_020_chunk_03].

Fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging is also used, where blue light is used to take a picture of the retina [nei_020_chunk_03].

Genetic testing can be suggested to learn more about the type of RP and predict how symptoms may change over time [nei_020_chunk_03].

This is general education, not a diagnosis.

This is general education, not a diagnosis.
